posts.note: Essay on reassurance-seeking in OCD. Only habitual generalizations ('will reliably reassure'); no call about a future state.
Review of the McGirr 2025 iTBS plus d-cycloserine OCD trial; three open-ended field-direction calls.
Reflection on informed consent for rapid remission after SAINT-style TMS. Hypotheticals about patients' lives and one normative close; no forecasts.
Three author statements plus four quoted press-release findings logged with own_claim false (author says he did not write the press release but co-authored the white paper).
Humorous essay about Fruit Logistica invitations; two low-value personal or joke expectations logged.
Mostly retrospective legal analysis of the DOJ qui tam case and advice to UnitedHealth (normative, not logged); one hedged legal-exposure call.
Personal essay on aging. Truisms such as 'Soon, all of my friends will also be old' not logged.
Author suspects he has tardive dyskinesia; own-tool publication timing, personal plans, and a Cobenfy safety claim logged.
Long educational post on antipsychotics and tardive syndromes; normative prescribing advice not logged.
Review of a negative knee osteoarthritis aiTBS trial; two borderline calls about sham design.

statements.quote: just this past month we have networks for psychosis, and more is coming
statements.context: Author describes lesion network mapping and connectome work (Mike Fox, Sean Siddiqi, Shan Siddiqi) that has produced functional network targets for depression, anxiety, PTSD and, this past month, psychosis. He asserts that more such network targets are coming.
statements.note: Vague, open-ended call about further network-mapping targets for new disorders.

statements.quote: I think these two lines of evidence, taken together, will allow a more effective discipline to emerge.
statements.context: Author's synthesis: two lines of evidence, connectome-based fMRI targeting and iTBS combined with pro-plasticity drugs like d-cycloserine, will together let a more effective brain-stimulation discipline emerge.
statements.note: Field-direction call without a date.

statements.quote: iTBS on its own would be a remarkable, game changing OCD treatment
statements.context: Commenting on the McGirr et al. 2025 American Journal of Psychiatry trial of iTBS plus d-cycloserine for treatment-refractory OCD (large effect sizes), the author asserts iTBS alone would be a game-changing OCD treatment and the combination even better. He notes the treatment is available at Fermata in NYC now.
statements.note: Evaluative claim with an implicit future-impact reading; borderline. Author's clinic offers the treatment (possible CONTROL).

statements.quote: Even if we had a cure for depression, tomorrow, that worked 100% of the time, I'm still not sure if we can get it paid for in a decade.
statements.context: Author's framing before sharing the BrainFutures / Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics press release: psychedelic medicine is exciting but not here yet, the market forces needed to bring it to the world are complicated, and even a perfect depression cure might not get paid for within a decade.
entities: Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics
statements.note: Conditional, hedged pessimism about payer adoption speed; applies to psychedelic medicine by context.

statements.quote: I've been hustling for more appropriate payment for transcranial magnetic stimulation for years, and we still have a long way to go.
statements.context: Same framing paragraph about healthcare payment complexity; the author says TMS payment reform still has a long way to go after years of his advocacy.
statements.confidence_phrase: still have a long way to go
statements.note: Implicit call that appropriate TMS payment remains distant; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: I'm hosting the next edition of Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment in Los Angeles on May 18th!
statements.context: Closing plug: the author will host the next Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment (RAMHT) conference in Los Angeles on May 18 (2025), with sponsors BrainFutures, MDHub.ai, GrayMatters Health and Simple Practice; tickets available now.
statements.note: Own-event announcement; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Half of survey respondents plan to add new psychedelic therapies to their practice within six months following FDA approval. However, 60 percent of respondents anticipate barriers to insurance coverage of psychedelic therapy.
statements.context: From the BrainFutures / CEP press release (which the author says he did not write) about the white paper 'Scaling Psychedelic Therapies in the Health System' that he co-authored: survey of mental health providers in 15 states on plans to adopt psychedelic therapy after FDA approval and expected insurance barriers.
statements.horizon_text: within six months following FDA approval
entities: Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics
statements.note: Quoted press-release survey finding; respondents' expectations, not the author's own call. Author co-authored the underlying white paper.

statements.quote: 30 percent of surveyed providers believe that insurance is very unlikely to cover psychedelic therapies, while only 5 percent believe that it is very likely to offer coverage.
statements.context: Additional finding listed in the BrainFutures / CEP press release: provider expectations about insurance coverage of psychedelic therapies.
entities: Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics
statements.note: Third-party survey result quoted in a press release the author shares.

statements.quote: Respondents are most likely to offer psilocybin to patients if it is FDA approved (60 percent), followed by ketamine (50 percent) and MDMA (40 percent).
statements.context: Additional finding in the press release: which psychedelic therapies providers would offer if FDA approved; the release notes only ketamine is currently FDA approved.
statements.note: Third-party survey result; conditional on FDA approval.

statements.quote: Health providers also described operational barriers that may limit access— including behavioral health workforce shortages and insurance challenges. That's why BrainFutures is building tools and other resources to support implementation after FDA approval.
statements.context: Quote attributed to BrainFutures executive director Sarah Norman in the press release: operational barriers may limit access to psychedelic therapy, and BrainFutures is building implementation tools for the period after FDA approval.
statements.note: Third-party quote; the author shares it without explicit endorsement beyond co-authoring the white paper.

statements.quote: I have to believe there will be fruit as a snack at several of these events.
statements.context: Humorous essay about repeated invitations to Fruit Logistica (Berlin, February 2026) caused by a name clash between the author's clinic Fermata and an Israeli agtech company; the author imagines the event and expects fruit snacks.
statements.confidence_phrase: I have to believe there will be
statements.note: Joke-framed, trivial expectation; logged for recall only.

statements.quote: I don't know; we'll see, but if I'm free next February, I might have to drop into Berlin and my colleagues at Fruit Logistica to figure out what's happening.
statements.context: Closing of the Fruit Logistica essay; the author says he was kidding at first but the event looks exciting, and he might attend Fruit Logistica in Berlin in February 2026 if free.
statements.note: Hedged personal plan; own activity, low forecast value.

statements.quote: there are additional investigations happening right now for other conduct on their part in other places that may meet the level of criminal or civil liability
statements.context: After congratulating UnitedHealth Group on a federal Special Master's recommendation to dismiss the DOJ Medicare Advantage upcoding qui tam case (UHC of California, 2009-2016 conduct), the author cautions that other ongoing investigations into UnitedHealth may result in criminal or civil liability.
statements.note: Hedged legal-exposure call about pending investigations.

statements.quote: I can't even tell you how well yet, because it hasn't been published yet. It should be available shortly.
statements.context: Author describes the tardive dyskinesia video-screening algorithm he built with Anthony Sterns (iRxReminder) and Videra Health, trained on hundreds of rated videos; he says it performed remarkably well, and the results (publication) should be available shortly. The tool is already offered at TDscreen.ai.
statements.note: Own-organization publication timing; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I have to go see a movement disorders doctor, myself. And maybe, these new medication's have written about it will be really helpful.
statements.context: Author suspects he has tardive dyskinesia (involuntary mouth movement) after years of antipsychotics for bipolar disorder; he plans to see a movement disorders specialist and speculates that the new TD medications (tetrabenazine, valbenazine) may help him.
statements.note: Personal health plan and hedged treatment expectation; low forecast value.

statements.quote: I'm gonna go from being a doctor to being a patient, and I will probably write about it, too.
statements.context: Author anticipates becoming a TD patient and writing about it in the newsletter; earlier in the post he also says he is sure he will not be able to stop talking about this for years.
statements.note: Newsletter content promise; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: That's why I'm excited about medicines like Cobenfy—the very first novel and psychotic that doesn't cause weight gain—and doesn't cause movement disorders, and that's available for people with psychosis now.
statements.context: Closing argument for safer options than dopamine-blocking antipsychotics; the author praises Cobenfy as the first novel antipsychotic that causes neither weight gain nor movement disorders and is available now for psychosis.
statements.note: Present-tense drug safety claim with an implicit long-term prediction (no movement disorders); borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: there are vastly more primary care doctors than there will ever be psychiatrists. This is even more true for children. Those primary care doctors are going to see patients suffering, and they're gonna try to help. They will try to help with tools at their disposal, which are overwhelmingly not psychotherapy.
statements.context: Argument that primary care will keep carrying most psychiatric prescribing: primary care doctors will always outnumber psychiatrists, especially for children, and will reach for non-psychotherapy tools (pills), which sets up the long-term movement-disorder risk the post explains.
statements.confidence_phrase: will ever be; are going to; will
statements.note: Compound structural claim; near-truism about workforce supply and prescribing behavior.

statements.quote: This tool, which will be published in the scientific literature soon, is probably my most important contribution to science yet.
statements.context: TDscreen.ai, the 90-second AI screening tool for tardive dyskinesia built with iRxReminder and Videra Health with NIH funding support, will be published in the scientific literature soon.
statements.note: Restates the previous day's 'should be available shortly' call; own organization, coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I've been working for several years, as I wrote yesterday , on an AI algorithm that will help screen for these movement disorders with vastly greater simplicity. It's a screening tool that exists now.
statements.context: Section 'How Can We Screen for TD?': the author says the AI algorithm will help screen for movement disorders with far greater simplicity; the tool exists now and health professionals can download it.
statements.note: Utility claim about the author's own tool; borderline forward-looking. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: This includes a vastly broader use of transcranial magnetic stimulation and other neuromodulatory approaches, of which more are coming to market soon.
statements.context: Summary section: the author advocates safer non-medication treatment for depression, including much broader TMS use and other neuromodulatory approaches, and asserts more such approaches are coming to market soon.
statements.note: Vague market-entry call for neuromodulation devices.

statements.quote: write to the manufacturer and request a sham coil. They'll probably hook you up.
statements.context: Critique of the Hodkinson et al. 2025 knee osteoarthritis aiTBS trial, which used 30% stimulator output as sham; the author advises future fMRI-guided TMS investigators to request a proper sham coil from the manufacturer and predicts they will probably provide one.
statements.note: Advice with a hedged prediction about manufacturer behavior; low forecast value.

statements.quote: It may be that 30% powered iTBS is enough to have a treatment effect! That could be why there is no separation between these two groups, as both were effectively active. I have reasons to doubt this is the case.
statements.context: Author weighs whether the 30%-output sham in the knee osteoarthritis trial was itself active, which would explain the lack of separation from active fMRI-guided aiTBS; he doubts it while noting it is not impossible.
statements.note: Doubt about a scientific hypothesis; implicit call about what a better-controlled replication would show. Borderline forward-looking.
